lesson.title: Corners, Cusps, and Cliffs: When the Derivative Does Not Exist
lesson.summary: The second way a critical number can arise is a point in the domain where the derivative simply does not exist, typically at a sharp corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent, illustrated here with x^(2/3) and x^(1/3).
lesson.body:
A derivative can fail to exist at a point for several familiar reasons, sharp corners, cusps, vertical tangent lines, or a break in the function itself. As long as the input value where this happens is still in the domain of the function, meaning the function actually has a value there even though it has no well defined tangent slope there, that input value counts as a critical number by the second half of the definition. If the point is not even in the domain, it is simply not part of the function at all, and it cannot be a critical number of that function.

Consider g(x) = x^(2/3). Its domain is every real number, since squaring first and then taking a cube root, or the reverse order, produces a real, non negative result no matter the sign of x. Differentiate with the power rule: g'(x) = (2/3)x^(-1/3), which can be rewritten as g'(x) = 2 / (3 times the cube root of x). At x = 0, the cube root of 0 is 0, putting a zero in the denominator, so g'(0) is undefined. Since x = 0 is in the domain of g, it qualifies as a critical number. Geometrically, as x approaches 0 from the positive side, the cube root of x approaches 0 through positive values, so g'(x) grows without bound toward positive infinity; approaching from the negative side, the cube root of x approaches 0 through negative values, so g'(x) plunges toward negative infinity. The tangent slopes are racing off in opposite directions on the two sides, which is exactly what a cusp, a sharp point on the graph, looks like. Notice also that g(x) = x^(2/3) is never negative, and it equals 0 only at x = 0, so this critical number turns out to be both a local and a global minimum, a fact confirmed properly once the First Derivative Test is introduced.

Now contrast that with h(x) = x^(1/3), the plain cube root function, whose domain is also every real number. Its derivative is h'(x) = (1/3)x^(-2/3), which can be rewritten as h'(x) = 1 / (3 times the square of the cube root of x). At x = 0 the denominator is again 0, so h'(0) is undefined, making x = 0 a critical number here as well. But look at the sign of h'(x) away from 0: the square of the cube root of x is positive for every x except 0, since a square can never be negative, so h'(x) is positive on both sides of 0, with no sign change at all. A positive derivative on both sides means h is increasing right through x = 0, the graph has a vertical tangent line there, a moment of infinite slope, but it never turns around. So x = 0 is a critical number of x^(1/3) that is not a local extremum, the same kind of false alarm as the x^3 example from the section on critical points, only this time triggered by a derivative that fails to exist rather than one that equals zero.

Between this section and the last one, every possible source of a critical number has now been covered: f'(c) = 0, or f'(c) undefined, always with c required to be in the domain. What is still missing is a dependable way to decide, for any critical number found through either doorway, whether it is a genuine local maximum, a genuine local minimum, or a false alarm like x = 0 for x^3 or for x^(1/3). Building that dependable test is the job of the First Derivative Test, next.
